cards.q: Which command shows the current directory (both PowerShell and Linux)?
cards.a: pwd (PowerShell: also Get-Location).

figure.alt: Side-by-side Linux and PowerShell pwd screenshots
figure.caption: pwd shows your current directory
figure.shows: Linux prints /home/student. PowerShell pwd (Get-Location) prints C:\Users\student. Same idea on both systems.

cards.q: How do you list files in the current folder? (PowerShell vs Arch)
cards.a: PowerShell: dir / ls / Get-ChildItem. Arch: ls (or ls -la for details).

figure.caption: ls lists files in the current folder
figure.shows: Short ls then detailed ls -la. PowerShell: dir / Get-ChildItem.

cards.q: How do you go up one level, and how do you go to the home directory?
cards.a: Up: cd ..  | Home: cd ~ (on Linux also just cd). PowerShell: also cd $HOME.

cards.q: How do you create a folder (and several subfolders) in the terminal?
cards.a: mkdir foldername. PowerShell: also New-Item -ItemType Directory. Arch: mkdir -p path/{a,b} for several at once.

cards.q: What does a pipe (|) do in the terminal?
cards.a: Sends output from one command as input to the next (e.g. find | grep hello, or Get-ChildItem | Where-Object).

figure.caption: Pipe | sends output to the next command
figure.shows: Left command stdout becomes right command stdin.

cards.q: What does chmod 600 mean on a Linux file?
cards.a: Owner gets read+write (rw-------); group/others get no access. r=4, w=2, x=1.

cards.q: Why does SHA256 change when you change a file?
cards.a: The checksum is a fingerprint of the whole contents; any change yields a new hash. Used to verify ISOs (SHA256SUMS).

figure.caption: Any change yields a new hash fingerprint
figure.shows: sha256sum changes completely when the file changes.

cards.q: Which key is the Host key in VirtualBox (to release the mouse pointer)?
cards.a: Right Ctrl.

cards.q: How do you ping 1.1.1.1 with a limited number of packets on Linux?
cards.a: ping -c 4 1.1.1.1 (otherwise stop with Ctrl+C). PowerShell: ping 1.1.1.1 (often 4 attempts by default).

figure.caption: Ping uses ICMP at the network layer
figure.shows: OSI Network layer (layer 3). Linux: ping -c 4 limits packets.
figure.attribution: Source: Wikimedia Commons (Public domain / CC0) - Offnfopt

cards.q: How do you search for and install the package tree on Arch?
cards.a: Search: pacman -Ss tree. Install: sudo pacman -S tree. Update the database first: sudo pacman -Sy. (Ubuntu/Kali later: apt update / apt install).

cards.q: How do you show the contents of a text file in the terminal?
cards.a: Arch: cat file.txt. PowerShell: Get-Content / type file.txt.

cards.q: How do you append a line to a file without deleting what is already there?
cards.a: Arch: echo "text" >> file.txt. PowerShell: "text" | Add-Content file.txt. (A single > / Set-Content overwrites.)

figure.caption: >> appends; > overwrites
figure.shows: echo a > file overwrites; echo b >> file appends.

cards.q: Which commands copy, move/rename, and delete a file? (PowerShell vs bash)
cards.a: bash: cp, mv, rm. PowerShell: Copy-Item, Move-Item, Remove-Item. Practise only inside a practice folder - rm -rf / -Recurse is dangerous.

figure.caption: List first - then copy, move or delete

cards.q: How do you find files under a folder and filter names with 'hello' on Arch?
cards.a: find ~/terminal-practice -type f | grep hello (count with | wc -l). PowerShell: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File | Where-Object Name -match 'hello'.

figure.caption: find/grep filter streams with pipes
figure.shows: Pipe into grep to keep matching lines.

cards.q: What does chmod 644 mean?
cards.a: Owner read+write; group and others read only (-rw-r--r--). Common for ordinary text files.

figure.caption: 644 is rw-r--r--
figure.shows: Owner write; others read. Compare with 600.

cards.q: How do you show the IPv4 address on Arch vs Windows?
cards.a: Arch: ip addr or ip -4 addr show (look for inet). Windows: ipconfig or Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4.

figure.caption: IP addressing lives at the network layer
figure.shows: OSI Network layer carries IP addresses.
figure.attribution: Source: Wikimedia Commons (Public domain / CC0) - Offnfopt

cards.q: Which command computes SHA256 for a file?
cards.a: Arch: sha256sum file. PowerShell: Get-FileHash file -Algorithm SHA256.

cards.q: How do you view command history and help?
cards.a: Arch: history | tail -20; man ls (quit with q). PowerShell: Get-History; Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Full.

cards.q: How do you interrupt a running command in a Linux terminal?
cards.a: Ctrl+C. (Copy/paste often: Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V.)

cards.q: According to Lecture 1 / the course outline: how many assignments, and what must you pass to sit the exam?
cards.a: At least 11 assignments will be given; at least 8 must be completed (pass) to qualify for the final exam. One-week deadlines are HARD. Pass/fail only - they do not count in the final grade. Labs still recommend Kali + Ubuntu/Windows VMs.

cards.q: What is the main focus of ACIT4050 according to the course plan?
cards.a: Practical and theoretical cybersecurity: penetration testing, cyber defence mechanisms, societal aspects, and the security - privacy relationship; real incidents are analysed.

cards.q: What do we defend according to Lecture 1, and what three properties does that require?
cards.a: Defend your systems so that no one can make them work contrary to your interests and intentions. That means maintaining Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (the CIA triad).

figure.caption: CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
figure.shows: Three classic security goals. Lab work trains all three.

cards.q: What does Confidentiality mean in Lecture 1's CIA triad?
cards.a: Protecting information from being accessed by unauthorized parties.

cards.q: What does Integrity mean in Lecture 1's CIA triad?
cards.a: Ensuring the authenticity of information - that information is not altered, and that the source of the information is genuine.

cards.q: What does Availability mean in Lecture 1's CIA triad?
cards.a: Information is accessible to authorized users.

cards.q: Authentication vs authorization - what is the difference?
cards.a: Authentication: verify who you are (prove identity). Authorization: decide what you may do after you are authenticated.

cards.q: What is an attack surface (lab / system sense)?
cards.a: The set of points where an attacker can try to enter or extract data (open services, interfaces, files, accounts, networks). Reducing unnecessary exposure shrinks it.

cards.q: What does sudo do on Linux?
cards.a: Runs a command with elevated privileges (typically as root) after authorization. Use sparingly; prefer ordinary user for daily work.

cards.q: How do you show the current user and host name?
cards.a: Linux: whoami and hostname. PowerShell: $env:USERNAME and $env:COMPUTERNAME (or whoami / hostname where available).

cards.q: Absolute vs relative path - what is the difference?
cards.a: Absolute starts from the root (e.g. /home/user/file or C:\Users\...). Relative is from the current directory (e.g. ./notes or ..\parent).

figure.caption: Absolute path from root; relative from here
figure.shows: pwd shows absolute path. cd Documents is relative.

cards.q: What does ls -la show that plain ls often hides?
cards.a: Long listing including permissions, owner, size, time, and usually hidden files (names starting with .).

figure.caption: ls -la shows permissions and hidden files
figure.shows: Mode bits like -rw------- appear in the listing.

cards.q: How do you search for text inside a file on Windows PowerShell vs Linux?
cards.a: PowerShell: findstr word file.txt or Select-String. Linux: grep word file.txt.

cards.q: What is the difference between > and >> when writing to a file?
cards.a: Single > overwrites (or creates) the file. Double >> appends without deleting existing content. PowerShell: Set-Content vs Add-Content.

cards.q: What is a package manager, and which ones does the course material prepare you for?
cards.a: Tool to search/install/update software packages safely. Arch cyberlab: pacman. Ubuntu/Kali later: apt (sudo apt update / apt install).

cards.q: What does ping test?
cards.a: Reachability/latency to a host using ICMP echo (network layer). Limited count on Linux: ping -c 4 host.

figure.caption: Ping checks reachability with ICMP echoes
figure.shows: Successful replies mean the host answered.

cards.q: What PC/VM resources does the ACIT4050 course plan recommend for labs?
cards.a: At least one Kali and one Ubuntu or Windows VM at once. Minimum guide: 4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, about 100-120 GB free disk. Basic Linux skills (packages, simple commands) are expected.

cards.q: What is the ACIT4050 final exam format (Lecture 1 course outline)?
cards.a: Final written exam - no supporting material permitted. Graded A to F. You must have completed at least 8 of the (at least 11) assignments to qualify.

cards.q: According to the ACIT4050 learning outcomes, what relationship should you be able to describe?
cards.a: The relationship between security and privacy, plus societal aspects of cybersecurity and cyber governance problems.

figure.alt: Security and privacy in course focus
figure.caption: Security and privacy together

cards.q: Name two practical skill areas highlighted in the ACIT4050 course introduction.
cards.a: Penetration testing and cyber defence mechanisms (plus analysing real incidents and explaining them to experts and non-experts).

cards.q: How do you often copy/paste in a Linux terminal without interrupting Ctrl+C?
cards.a: Ctrl+Shift+C to copy and Ctrl+Shift+V to paste (Ctrl+C interrupts the running process).

cards.q: How does Lecture 1 (citing Peltier) distinguish information security from cyber security?
cards.a: Information security uses physical and logical access controls so data and information assets are used properly and not unauthorizedly modified, destroyed, disclosed, lost, or accessed (automated or manual records/files) - plus legal barriers. Cyber security is the subset limited to information stored on computers or communicated between computers.

cards.q: What is the hierarchy of trust for a computer system (Lecture 1)?
cards.a: Entities trust themselves and all technology layers below them. Other trust relations should be imposed by a higher-layer entity, a user, a systems manager, and/or cryptographic protocols.

cards.q: Who maintains the hierarchy of trust for software vs for the instruction set and below?
cards.a: Software: the companies that developed it (security mistakes fixed via software updates). Instruction set and below: component manufacturers and system integrators (firmware updates when possible).

cards.q: For the software (upper) layers in the hierarchy of trust, who maintains trust and how are discovered security mistakes corrected?
cards.a: Maintained by the software companies that developed it. Discovered security mistakes are corrected through software security updates.

cards.q: List the hierarchy of trust technology layers from top to bottom (Lecture 1).
cards.a: 1) Application 2) Operating System 3) Hardware Adaptation Layer (HAL) 4) Instruction set 5) Integrated circuits for memory, processing and communication 6) Logic gates 7) Transistors 8) Physical phenomena. Device drivers span the OS and HAL.

cards.q: Where do device drivers sit in the Lecture 1 hierarchy of trust stack?
cards.a: They span the Operating System and the Hardware Adaptation Layer (HAL) - beside both, not a separate numbered layer of their own.

cards.q: In the hierarchy of trust stack, which layers are the upper software-oriented part vs the lower hardware/physics part?
cards.a: Upper: Application, Operating System (with device drivers), and Hardware Adaptation Layer. Lower: Instruction set, integrated circuits, logic gates, transistors, and physical phenomena.

cards.q: What must not interfere with each other in unauthorized ways (separation of untrusted entities)?
cards.a: Processes, applications, users, and instances of operating systems must not interfere with each other unauthorizedly.

cards.q: Name four responsibilities Lecture 1 assigns to system administrators and users for separating untrusted entities.
cards.a: Examples: healthy passwords; strong cryptography; admission control (physical and logical); system/firewall configuration; software and systems updates; installing only authorized software; care with mail attachments; not connecting to unauthorized hardware (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB).

cards.q: Who is responsible for separating operating systems on the same hardware, and what does that involve?
cards.a: The hypervisor (configured by the administrator): privileges in shared file systems, virtually separate file systems, process isolation support, and resource scheduling to avoid denial of service.

cards.q: In a networked environment, which protections does Lecture 1 list for administrators and users?
cards.a: Firewalls (allowed traffic); NATs (hide addresses/structure); VPNs (logically separate networks with different privileges); cryptographic protocols (integrity and confidentiality); redundancy, scheduling and capacity (availability).

cards.q: What are zero days, and where does Lecture 1 say most incidents come from?
cards.a: Zero days are security holes known to someone but not yet closed (or unpatched). Most incidents involve mistakes by users or system administrators; problems also arise from software/hardware developers and known holes without updates.

cards.q: Name Lecture 1's three classifications of infections (malware types by how infection spreads).
cards.a: Virus, Worms, and Trojans.

cards.q: What is a computer virus according to Lecture 1?
cards.a: Code that cannot live on its own: it attaches/inserts into a host program or file and runs whenever that host runs. It spreads by infecting other executables (often when the host is shared or executed). Initial infection can come from a once-run program (e.g. a link in e-mail).

cards.q: How does a worm differ from a virus (Lecture 1)?
cards.a: A worm is self-contained and needs no host file. It self-replicates across networks without altering existing executables, e.g. by exploiting OS vulnerabilities or via e-mail attachments/links that download and run it.

cards.q: What is a Trojan in Lecture 1's malware classification?
cards.a: Malware embedded in a seemingly legitimate/useful application that the user knowingly downloads and runs (screensaver, weather widget, fake virus scanner, e-mail attachment, or malicious web page). After that trust, the payload (e.g. backdoor) runs. Unlike viruses/worms, it typically does not self-replicate.

cards.q: How does a Trojan operate differently from a virus and a worm?
cards.a: Virus: needs a host program/file; spreads by attaching and when the host runs or is shared. Worm: standalone; self-replicates across networks with no host file. Trojan: appears legitimate/useful and tricks the user into installing/running it; typically does not self-replicate - the harm is the payload/backdoor after the user trusts it.

cards.q: How does Lecture 1 say detection differs for Trojans/worms vs viruses?
cards.a: Trojans and worms can be spotted via process/application lists. Viruses often require analysis of the infected program. Malicious actions may reveal any of them - sometimes too late.

cards.q: What is spyware according to Lecture 1 (classification by intent)?
cards.a: Its task is to collect sensitive information from the system it resides on and transfer it to the attacker - e.g. keystroke logging, analysing document contents, or analysing the system itself in preparation for future attacks.

cards.q: What is ransomware according to Lecture 1 (classification by intent)?
cards.a: Malware that puts the attacker in a position to require a ransom from the system owner. Most often by encrypting vital information and requiring compensation to make it available again.

cards.q: What is a rootkit according to Lecture 1 (classification by intent)?
cards.a: A set of techniques used to mask the presence of malware, usually via privileged root/administrator access. Not bad per se, but central to most sophisticated attacks; hard to detect/remove because they can subvert anti-malware tools.

cards.q: What is a bot and a botnet according to Lecture 1 (classification by intent)?
cards.a: A bot gives the attacker (botmaster) remote control of a system. A botnet is many infected machines under one botmaster - typically used to attack other computers or send spam.

cards.q: What are DoS and DDoS attacks according to Lecture 1?
cards.a: Denial of Service and Distributed Denial of Service. They target availability by overloading a target with requests or traffic. Usually performed with botnets where all bots flood the target at once. Targets are often web servers, but other servers too.

cards.q: Name the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (Lecture 1).
cards.a: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover, and Govern - the highest-level pillars of a holistic cybersecurity program.

cards.q: According to Lecture 1, how does AI change the NIST CSF functions?
cards.a: AI profoundly changes Detect and heavily influences Respond and Protect. It is a more generic tool for Identify, Recover, and Govern (and should not be solely responsible for Identify or Govern).

cards.q: In the NIST CSF 2.0 wheel (Lecture 1), where does Govern sit relative to the other functions?
cards.a: Govern is the inner surrounding ring - organisational governance wraps Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

cards.q: List the seven Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain stages from Lecture 1.
cards.a: 1) Reconnaissance 2) Weaponization 3) Delivery 4) Exploitation 5) Installation 6) Command and control 7) Action on objectives.

cards.q: Name the Lockheed Martin Kill Chain stages in order using the short slide labels.
cards.a: Recon, Weaponise, Deliver, Exploit, Install, C2, Action (left to right).

cards.q: Which Kill Chain stages does Lecture 1 say AI simplifies massively?
cards.a: Reconnaissance and Weaponization massively; Delivery to some extent; Exploitation massively via better recon/weaponization; Installation partly. C2 and Action on objectives are not directly driven by AI, though AI can help hide or detect protective actions.

cards.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK, and why does Lecture 1 point to it?
cards.a: An extended, more detailed kill-chain-style knowledge base (attack.mitre.org) with vulnerabilities, mitigations, and detection mechanisms - useful examples beyond the simplified Lockheed Martin chain.

cards.a: At least 11 assignments will be given; at least 8 must be completed to qualify for the exam. One-week deadlines are hard. Graded pass/fail only - they do not count toward the final course grade. Final exam: written, no supporting material, A-F.

cards.q: How do you open built-in documentation for a command?
cards.a: Linux: man ls (quit with q). PowerShell: Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Full.

cards.q: DoS vs DDoS (Lecture 1): how do they differ, and what do they share?
cards.a: Both target availability by overloading a target with requests/traffic (often web or other servers). DoS is the general Denial of Service idea (can be from a single source). DDoS is Distributed: usually a botnet where many bots flood the target simultaneously.

cards.q: Name Lecture 1's four malware classes according to intent.
cards.a: Spyware, Ransomware, Bot, and Rootkit - classified by what the malware is for (intent), not by how it spreads.

cards.q: Lecture 1: how does classification by intent differ from virus/worm/Trojan?
cards.a: Virus / worm / Trojan classify how infection spreads or is delivered. Spyware / ransomware / bot / rootkit classify intent (steal data, demand ransom, remote control, hide malware). The same sample can fit both axes (e.g. a Trojan that installs ransomware).

cards.q: Spyware vs ransomware (Lecture 1 intent classes) - contrast the goals.
cards.a: Spyware: collect sensitive info and transfer it to the attacker (keystrokes, documents, system prep for later attacks). Ransomware: force a ransom - most often encrypt vital info and demand payment to restore availability.

cards.q: Bot vs rootkit (Lecture 1 intent classes) - contrast the roles.
cards.a: Bot: remote control by a botmaster (many bots = botnet for attacks/spam). Rootkit: techniques to mask malware presence, usually with root/admin privileges - not bad per se, but central to sophisticated attacks and hard to detect/remove (can subvert anti-malware).

cards.q: Whose duty is separating processes/apps and users on one computer (Lecture 1)?
cards.a: The operating system (often configured by admin/user). For processes/apps: privileged file systems, memory mapping, CPU scheduling, peripheral virtualization. For users: passwords, privileges (e.g. root), separate file systems / access control, process isolation, resource scheduling against DoS.

cards.q: What is the purpose of phishing attacks (4050 exam-style / Lecture 2)?
cards.a: Trick a person into revealing credentials or installing malware so the attacker can steal data, money, or a foothold in systems - social engineering, not a protocol break.

cards.q: Phishing vs spear phishing vs whaling?
cards.a: Phishing: mass bait (email/SMS/web). Spear phishing: targeted at a chosen person/org with personal context. Whaling: spear phishing aimed at high-value targets (executives, finance leads).

cards.q: After a phishing message succeeds, how is information security compromised?
cards.a: Victim may enter credentials on a fake site, open a malicious attachment, or run an exploit kit. Stolen secrets or malware then give the attacker access to mail, accounts, or the target network.

cards.q: Which influence principles are often exploited in phishing messages?
cards.a: Cialdini-style levers: authority (fake boss/bank), urgency/scarcity (act now), social proof, liking/familiarity, reciprocity, and commitment/consistency (you already clicked once).

cards.q: What technological causes enable phishing in messaging?
cards.a: Anyone can send mail/SMS that looks official; sender identity is easy to spoof; HTML/images hide tracking pixels and fake login forms; users cannot reliably see the real URL or TLS identity.

cards.q: How does AI support phishing (4050 Lecture 2 readings)?
cards.a: Cheaper fluent text in many languages, personalised lures from public data, and deepfake voice (vishing) that can impersonate executives (Canvas links XOR Lab, Reuters, and a $240k voice-theft case).

cards.q: Name four organisational countermeasures against phishing.
cards.a: Examples: MFA; mail filtering/DMARC; disable automatic image load / pixel blocking; report-phish button; least privilege; simulated training (Gophish-style); do not reuse passwords on external sites.

cards.q: How is a phishing training platform used for awareness?
cards.a: Staff send simulated phish (e.g. Gophish), measure who clicks, then debrief. Goal is practice recognising lures, not punishing people. Listed with L03 / exploit-kit readings.

cards.q: What is an e-mail tracking pixel (4050 Lecture 2 / The Verge)?
cards.a: A tiny (often 1x1 transparent) image hosted on a remote server. Opening the mail downloads it, so the sender sees that the message was opened and can infer time, IP, and sometimes location.

cards.q: How does Gmail reduce tracking-pixel location leaks?
cards.a: Images are fetched via Google proxy servers. Open-tracking can still see that mail was read, but the tracker usually gets Google's IP, not yours, and less cookie leakage.

cards.q: What is the [A]pache phishing kit (Check Point report on Canvas)?
cards.a: A paid Dark Web kit ($100-300) that lets low-skill criminals clone fake shops (e.g. Walmart), import products, collect card/CVV in an admin panel, then show a fake payment-failed page.

cards.q: What is an exploit kit in the ACIT4050 L03 / Mokoena et al. context?
cards.a: Software that automates delivering browser/plugin exploits after a lure (often phishing). Victim visits a kit landing page; the kit tries known vulnerabilities and drops malware.

cards.q: CIA triad: eavesdropping on unencrypted email, or unauthorized access to personnel records?
cards.a: Confidentiality - the wrong party can see or hear data that should stay secret.

cards.q: CIA triad: a bug that alters financial data?
cards.a: Integrity - data is changed so it is no longer correct, even if nobody stole it.

cards.q: CIA triad: data-center fire that takes services down, or ransomware that makes files unusable?
cards.a: Availability - you cannot use the system or the files when you need them.

cards.q: Which activities sit under NIST CSF Identify?
cards.a: Asset inventory (hardware, software, data, people), mapping dependencies and critical services (including suppliers), and identifying cybersecurity risk to assets and capabilities.

cards.q: Encrypting data at rest, restoring after an outage, and incident-response communication - which NIST functions?
cards.a: Protect (encrypt), Recover (restore services), Respond (incident communication). None of these are Identify.
